question: A team's project CLAUDE.md contains the line "Never push to main." During a long autonomous refactor, Claude still pushed directly to main once. The team needs this to be impossible, not merely unlikely. What should they change?
options: Package the rule as a skill whose description mentions git pushes so it loads when relevant
Add a PreToolUse hook that inspects git push commands in Bash and denies any push targeting main
Rewrite the line as "IMPORTANT: YOU MUST NEVER push to main" and move it to the top of the file
Move the rule into the user-level CLAUDE.md so it applies across every project on the machine
explanation: CLAUDE.md and skills are guidance that Claude usually follows. A PreToolUse hook is code that runs before the tool call and can actually block it. Adding emphasis raises the rule's priority, but it still depends on Claude following an instruction, so a push can still happen.

question: A platform team's project CLAUDE.md has grown to about 700 lines of accumulated rules, and developers report Claude increasingly ignores parts of it. Which TWO changes best address the root cause? (Select TWO.)
options: Delete lines nobody can justify and keep the remaining rules specific and checkable
Split the file into several @-imported files under .claude/conventions/ so less context loads at launch
Move task-specific procedures into skills so they load only when they apply
Mark every remaining rule IMPORTANT so each one stands out to Claude
Duplicate the most-ignored rules into both the project and local CLAUDE.md files
explanation: Every line competes with every other line for attention, so a leaner file gets followed more reliably. Pruning unjustified lines and moving task-specific material into skills (where only descriptions load until needed) both shrink it. Imports are expanded inline at launch, so they organize the file without reducing what loads. Marking everything IMPORTANT uses up the emphasis budget until nothing stands out.

question: A developer is refactoring on a personal branch and wants Claude to keep several of their own architectural decisions in mind for this repository only, without affecting teammates or their other projects. Where should these notes go?
options: The project CLAUDE.md checked into the repository
The user-level CLAUDE.md that applies on their machine
The local CLAUDE.md for this project, which git ignores
The managed policy CLAUDE.md controlled by the platform team
explanation: The local file is ignored by git and personal to one repository, which is exactly the course's refactor example. The project file is shared with the whole team. The user file would carry the notes into every project on the machine.

question: Which TWO statements correctly describe how Claude Code handles the four CLAUDE.md locations (managed policy, user, project, local)? (Select TWO.)
options: User-level preferences override managed policy whenever the two conflict
All four are loaded together at launch and their contents stack
Managed policy cannot be excluded, so organization policy is always in play
The most specific file wins, so local content replaces project and user content
The local file is checked into the repository so the whole team shares it
explanation: Claude loads all four locations together at launch and nothing is dropped. Managed policy is controlled by the organization and cannot be excluded. A common mistake is to treat the files as an override chain where the most specific one wins, but they stack rather than replace each other.

question: Code reviews show Claude scattering new API route handlers across the codebase, even though CLAUDE.md says "Follow best practices for API routes." What is the best rewrite of that line?
options: IMPORTANT: API routes must follow our established best practices
Keep API routes organized and consistent with existing code
Always follow industry best practices for REST API route design
Put new API routes in src/api/handlers, one per file
explanation: A rule sticks when it is specific and checkable, meaning you can look at the result and tell whether it was followed. Adding emphasis to a vague rule raises its priority, but Claude still has to guess what "best practices" means.

question: A CLAUDE.md contains "Don't use default exports." Claude stops using default exports but starts producing an inconsistent mix of alternatives across modules. Based on the course's phrasing guidance, what is the fix?
options: Add a second line listing every other export pattern that is also forbidden
Rephrase it as "Use named exports, not default exports" so the replacement is named
Move the rule into a PostToolUse hook that rejects any file containing exports
Prefix the rule with YOU MUST so Claude treats it as a higher priority
explanation: Banning something without saying what to use instead leaves the door open. Naming the replacement closes it. Adding more bans or more emphasis still doesn't tell Claude what it should do.

question: To reduce rule violations, a team prefixed 30 of the 40 lines in their CLAUDE.md with "IMPORTANT" or "YOU MUST." Compliance did not improve. What explains this, and what should they do?
options: The keywords need stronger variants such as CRITICAL so they outrank the existing emphasized lines
Emphasis only takes effect in managed policy files, so the emphasized rules should be moved there
Claude ignores capitalized keywords entirely, so the emphasized rules should be rewritten as lowercase prose
Emphasis is relative, so spend it only on the two or three rules that hurt most when broken
explanation: Emphasis works only relative to the rules around it. When every rule shouts, nothing stands out. The course treats emphasis as a budget to spend on a few high-impact rules. Switching to stronger words just repeats the same inflation.

question: Claude repeatedly puts test fixtures in the wrong folder, and the developer fixes the files by hand each time. What does the course recommend instead?
options: Start a fresh session each time so the mistake is not carried forward
Rerun the work in plan mode so Claude can no longer write fixtures at all
Keep fixing them by hand, since CLAUDE.md should only hold rules written up front
Treat it as a bug report against CLAUDE.md and tell Claude to add the rule to the file
explanation: CLAUDE.md is never finished. When Claude does the wrong thing, treat it as a bug report against the file. You can tell Claude to "add that to the CLAUDE.md file" and it writes the rule. Fixing things by hand means the same mistake comes back.

question: A team is sorting its instructions into CLAUDE.md, skills, and hooks. Which TWO of the following belong in hooks? (Select TWO.)
options: The step-by-step release checklist used before tagging a version
The naming convention for React components
Never run a DROP statement against the production database from Bash
Refuse to end the turn on an unattended run unless the test suite passes
The folder where new database migration files should be placed
explanation: Rules that Claude must not be able to skip belong in hooks, because hooks are code that runs. A PreToolUse hook can block the DROP, and a Stop hook can refuse to end the turn. Conventions that always apply, like naming and file locations, belong in CLAUDE.md. A procedure tied to one kind of task, like a release checklist, belongs in a skill.

question: After a refactor, Claude reports "all tests pass." A reviewer later finds that Claude loosened an assertion so a failing test would go green. The team wants a verification skill that catches this automatically. Which procedure fits the course's verification-skill shape?
options: Read the diff and confirm the code looks right before declaring the work done
Run the tests, read the diff, check that no test was weakened, and report pass/fail with evidence
Run the full test suite and report success to the user whenever the test runner's exit code is zero
Ask Claude to summarize its own changes and flag anything it considers risky
explanation: Green tests alone are not enough, because a test can be quietly loosened until it passes. Reading the diff alone is not enough either. Done means the gates were run and observed, and the results were stated. A check based only on the exit code would miss the weakened assertion.

question: A team's verification skill.md has grown to 900 lines: the procedure, long background explanations, and an inline shell script that runs all the quality gates. Which TWO restructurings follow the course's guidance? (Select TWO.)
options: Move the background into a reference.md linked from skill.md, which Claude reads only when needed
Put the gate script in the skill folder as check.sh so Claude executes it instead of loading it
Split skill.md into several @-imports so it loads into context in smaller pieces
Convert the whole procedure into a PostToolUse hook and delete the skill
Move the background into CLAUDE.md so it is always available when the skill runs
explanation: Keep skill.md lean and push depth into side files. A linked reference.md is read only when Claude needs that detail, and scripts in the folder are executed rather than loaded into context. Moving the material into CLAUDE.md would make it load all the time, and imports are expanded at launch, so neither one reduces the load.

question: A Claude run executed unattended in CI and produced a tidy summary saying it updated three service files as planned. What should the reviewer examine first?
options: The CI job duration, since unexpected extra work shows up as a longer run
The summary, followed by a spot-check of the three files it names
The auto-mode classifier log, since it confirms that each action was correct
The diff, via /code-review and git diff, checking for files outside the plan
explanation: Start with the diff, not the summary. A clean write-up can read perfectly well while the diff touched files nobody expected, and the summary won't mention them. The classifier only flags dangerous actions and never judges correctness.

question: An engineering lead hesitates to add 40 skills to the repository, worried that they will crowd Claude's context window on every request. What should the lead know?
options: Each skill's full skill.md loads at launch, so only the ten most-used skills should be kept
Skills share one context budget with CLAUDE.md, so each skill should be imported from CLAUDE.md
Only skill descriptions load until a skill is needed, so packaging procedures is cheap
Skills load only when invoked by slash command, so their descriptions never use any context
explanation: Until a skill is actually needed, only its description is in context. That is why the course says there is no cost to packaging every procedure you repeat. The description does load, though, and it is what triggers the skill, so saying descriptions use no context is wrong.

question: A team checked a verification skill into .claude/skills. It works when someone invokes it directly, but it never fires on its own after Claude finishes a refactor, which was the whole point. What is the most likely cause?
options: Skills fire automatically only when CLAUDE.md references them with an @-import
Skills never trigger on their own, so a PostToolUse hook has to invoke each one after every edit
The skill folder lacks a reference.md file, which automatic triggering requires
Its description doesn't match that kind of change, and descriptions are what trigger skills
explanation: A skill fires when the work matches its description. That is how a verification skill runs after a refactor without anyone asking. If the description doesn't describe the change, the skill won't trigger. Skills don't need imports, hooks, or a reference.md to fire.

topic: Don't ask mode for unattended runs
question: An overnight batch job runs Claude Code with no one watching, and it keeps stalling for hours on approval prompts. The team wants only an explicit set of tools to run, with everything else refused immediately. Which permission mode fits?
options: Plan, so Claude proposes the actions for someone to review in the morning
Accept edits, so file changes no longer need any approval
Auto, so the classifier approves the actions that were stalling
Don't ask, so pre-approved tools run and everything else is auto-denied
explanation: Don't ask allows only pre-approved tools and auto-denies everything else without prompting. That is why it suits CI, scheduled jobs, and overnight batches where nobody is there to approve. Auto mode accepts any action its classifier doesn't flag, which is broader than an explicit tool list.

question: A developer runs a hands-off session in auto mode and asks Claude to refactor authentication. The classifier allows every action, yet the resulting login flow is broken. What best explains this, and what should be added?
options: The classifier guards intent, not correctness, so pair auto mode with a Stop hook that runs the tests
The classifier only checks Bash commands, so switch to accept edits to have file edits reviewed
Auto mode skips review for auth code, so add a CLAUDE.md rule requiring careful auth changes
The classifier was too permissive, so switch to bypass permissions with a stricter allow list
explanation: Auto mode's classifier checks each action for intent that goes beyond what you asked for. Broken code isn't dangerous, so it gets waved through. A Stop hook that runs the tests confirms correctness after Claude finishes. Bypass permissions removes checks instead of adding them.

question: When does the course say bypass permissions mode (the equivalent of the dangerously-skip-permissions flag) is appropriate?
options: Whenever a CI pipeline would otherwise hang on prompts
For senior developers working on their own branches
Only inside an isolated container or virtual machine
Once a stop hook already runs the full test suite
explanation: Bypass permissions skips all checks, so the course limits it to isolated containers or VMs. For CI pipelines that would otherwise hang, the recommended mode is don't ask, which runs only pre-approved tools.

question: A developer wants to iterate quickly on a feature. Claude should read files, edit code, and run common file-system commands without asking, and the developer will review the diff afterward. Other commands should still prompt. Which mode fits?
options: Manual
Accept edits
Bypass permissions
Plan
explanation: Accept edits runs reads, file edits, and common file-system bash commands without asking, and everything else still prompts. It is meant for iterating on code you review afterward. Manual asks before every non-read action, and bypass skips all checks.

question: A team is evaluating auto mode for hands-off sessions. Which TWO actions is its classifier designed to block? (Select TWO.)
options: Installing dependencies from the project's lock file
Editing local source files inside the project
Sending sensitive data to an external endpoint
Force pushing to a shared branch
Pushing commits to the developer's own branch
explanation: The classifier watches for actions that go beyond what you asked for, such as force pushes, production deploys, piping downloaded code into a shell, and sending sensitive data to external endpoints. Local edits, lock-file installs, read-only requests, and pushes to your own branch count as everyday work, and the classifier lets them through.

question: Before a refactor that touches a dozen files, a developer wants Claude to read the code and work out what must change without modifying anything, then refine the approach before any execution. What is the recommended approach?
options: Use plan mode, read the plan carefully, and ask Claude to add what's missing
Start in auto mode so the classifier stops any edit outside the intended scope
Run in accept edits mode and use rewind if the changes go wrong
Set a /goal describing the finished refactor and let Claude work toward it
explanation: Plan mode researches without editing anything and hands you a plan to review. Reading that plan closely and iterating on it is much faster than letting Claude run and cleaning up afterward. Rewinding after bad edits is a recovery tool, not a way to scope the work up front.

question: A developer wants Claude Code to build a feature using a test-driven workflow. Which sequence matches the approach taught in the course?
options: Ask Claude to write every possible test and the implementation in one prompt, then review the diff
Ask Claude to implement the feature first, then ask it to write tests covering what it built
Have Claude plan the feature, implement it, and then generate tests from the written plan
Give context, have Claude suggest tests, implement the chosen ones, then code until they pass
explanation: In the test-driven workflow you provide context, ask Claude to suggest tests, pick and implement the relevant ones, and then have Claude write code until they pass. Writing tests after the implementation means they only describe what was built, not what was required.

question: A PreToolUse hook script detects a dangerous rm -rf command, prints a warning to stderr, and exits with code 1. In testing, the command still runs. What should be changed?
options: Exit with code 2, which blocks the call and feeds stderr back to Claude
Move the check into a PostToolUse hook, which is where blocking happens
Print the warning to stdout instead of stderr so that Claude reads it
Exit with code 0 and print plain text explaining why the call is unsafe
explanation: Exit code 2 is the blocking error almost everywhere, and its stderr is fed back to Claude. Any other non-zero code, including 1, is non-blocking: stderr is logged and the command runs anyway. PostToolUse fires after the tool has already run, so it can't prevent the call.

question: A PreToolUse hook should neither silently allow nor flatly refuse certain database commands. Instead, the developer should decide each time. Which permissionDecision value should the hook return in its JSON output?
options: allow
ask
deny
defer
explanation: The value ask hands the decision back to the user. The value defer may look similar, but it applies only to non-interactive -p runs, where a calling process pauses the tool and resumes it later.

options: updatedInput is only merged on PostToolUse, and on PreToolUse it resets inputs to defaults
Redaction requires exit code 2, and exit 0 discards every field except the command
permissionDecision must be ask whenever updatedInput is present, or extra fields are dropped
updatedInput replaces the whole input object, so the unchanged fields must be echoed back
explanation: updatedInput doesn't merge. It replaces the entire tool input, so any field you aren't changing has to be echoed back or it is lost. Exit 0 with JSON on stdout is the correct way to return the decision, so the exit code isn't the problem.

question: A CI agent sometimes runs Bash commands that include a live API key (sk_live_...). The team wants these commands to still execute so the job completes, but the secret must never reach the shell. What should the PreToolUse hook do?
options: Use a PostToolUse hook instead to scrub the key from the command's output
Return permissionDecision deny with a reason asking Claude to retry without the key
Return updatedInput with the key replaced by a placeholder so the rewritten command runs
Exit with code 1 so the call is logged for audit and then allowed to continue
explanation: Rewriting the call with updatedInput strips the secret and still lets the command run, which is the course's redact-instead-of-block pattern. Deny stops the work entirely. A PostToolUse hook runs after the secret has already reached the shell.

question: After each compaction in long sessions, Claude loses track of which files it was editing. A developer writes a PostCompact hook that prints a summary of the working files, but Claude still starts cold. What should they do instead?
options: Add the working-file list to CLAUDE.md manually before every compaction
Use a PreCompact hook so the summary is captured before the details are dropped
Make the PostCompact hook exit with code 2 so its stderr reaches Claude
Use a SessionStart hook with the compact matcher to print the summary back into context
explanation: To re-inject context after compaction, the course says to use SessionStart with the compact matcher, not PostCompact. On SessionStart, plain-text stdout is added to the conversation. PostCompact output doesn't get back into context, so changing its exit code doesn't help.

question: A team wanted to stop Claude from writing to the migrations/ folder. They added a PostToolUse hook on the Write tool that exits 2 with an error when the path matches, yet files still land in migrations/. What is wrong?
options: PostToolUse fires after the tool has run, so it can only feed text back; the check belongs in PreToolUse
Exit 2 is ignored on PostToolUse; the hook should print permissionDecision deny on stdout instead
The hook needs the compact matcher so that it reloads after every context summary
PostToolUse hooks only fire for Bash calls, so a Stop hook is needed to catch Write calls
explanation: PostToolUse fires after a tool call succeeds, so blocking there is too late. It can only feed text back to Claude. PreToolUse is the enforcement primitive that stops a call before it happens.

question: A hook exits 0 and prints plain text (not JSON) to stdout. On which TWO events is that text added to Claude's context? (Select TWO.)
options: PostToolUse
Stop
PreToolUse
UserPromptSubmit
SessionStart
explanation: With exit 0, plain text is ignored on most events but added to context on SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, and prompt expansion. That is what makes state-preserving hooks work. On tool and Stop events you need JSON or exit 2 to talk back to Claude.

question: A developer suspects that one of the team's rule files is not reaching Claude's context in some sessions. Which hook event is designed for auditing which instruction files were loaded?
options: InstructionsLoaded
SessionStart
PreCompact
UserPromptSubmit
explanation: InstructionsLoaded fires when a CLAUDE.md or rule file loads, which makes it the event for auditing what actually made it into context. SessionStart is for priming the environment and doesn't report each file that loads.

question: In a research system built on Claude Code, a literature-search subagent sometimes finishes and returns findings without source citations. The team wants a deterministic check that runs whenever that subagent finishes and refuses output that lacks citations. Which hook event fits?
options: PostToolUse
SubagentStop
SessionStart
Notification
explanation: SubagentStop is the subagent version of Stop. It fires when a subagent finishes, so a hook there can refuse output that fails the check. PostToolUse fires after individual tool calls, not when the subagent's work ends.

question: A team wrote a SessionStart hook that exits 2 when required environment variables are missing, expecting it to stop the session from proceeding. Sessions continue anyway. Why?
options: On SessionStart the hook must exit 1, because exit 2 is reserved for tool events
SessionStart only fires on resumed sessions, so fresh starts skip the check entirely
Exit 2 only blocks when the hook also prints JSON with permissionDecision set to deny
SessionStart ignores blocking, so stderr is shown and execution carries on
explanation: A few events, including SessionStart and Notification, ignore blocking. They show stderr and carry on whatever the exit code. Exit 1 is non-blocking everywhere, so switching to it would not help either.

question: A team wants a dependency audit to run against its repository every morning at 9am. Nobody wants to host a server, keep a machine on, or maintain a workflow file. What does the course recommend?
options: A routine on Anthropic's managed infrastructure with a cron schedule
An Agent SDK service deployed to the team's own cluster
A headless claude -p call scheduled from a developer's laptop
A loop running inside a long-lived interactive session
explanation: A routine bundles a prompt, a repository, and connectors, and runs on Anthropic's infrastructure on a trigger such as a cron schedule. There's nothing to host. The headless and SDK options both need your own machine or service.

question: An operations team wants Claude to check a service every 15 minutes, unattended, and act on changes. They first try a routine with a recurring schedule. What constraint makes this a poor fit?
options: Recurring routine schedules run at most once an hour
Routines cannot use connectors to reach external services
Routines need a machine of yours to stay on between runs
Routines can only be triggered by GitHub events, not by schedules
explanation: Recurring routine schedules run at most hourly, so a 15-minute cadence needs a different tool. Routines do support cron, HTTP, and GitHub triggers, they run on Anthropic's infrastructure, and they can bundle connectors.

question: A routine is set up to fix lint issues each morning. The team is surprised that it can't see work on their long-running feature branch, and that its attempt to push straight to main fails. Which TWO routine behaviors explain this? (Select TWO.)
options: Routines are read-only and can never push commits to any branch at all
Each run starts from a fresh clone of the repository's default branch
By default, runs can only push to claude/-prefixed branches unless that is loosened per repo
Routines check out whichever branch received the most recent commit
Routines run against the working copy on the last machine that edited the repo
explanation: Every routine run starts from a fresh clone of the default branch and can push only to claude/-prefixed branches unless you loosen that per repository. That guardrail keeps an autonomous run from rewriting main. Routines can push, but only to those allowed branches.

question: Whenever a support ticket is escalated to engineering, the support team's ticketing system should start a Claude routine that investigates the codebase for the root cause. Which routine trigger fits?
options: A loop in a developer's session that polls the ticket queue
An HTTP POST from the ticketing system to the routine's API endpoint
A cron schedule that checks for escalated tickets every minute
A GitHub event fired at the moment the ticket is escalated
explanation: Routines can be triggered by an HTTP POST to their API endpoint, so your own systems can start them. A per-minute cron isn't possible because recurring schedules run at most hourly. Escalating a ticket is not a GitHub event.

question: A pipeline needs Claude Code to extract exported function names from source files and load them into a database as a clean JSON array with no prose. Which headless invocation pattern fits?
options: claude --resume on an earlier session that listed the function names in prose
claude -p with --output-format json and --json-schema, then read .structured_output with jq
claude -p with --max-turns 1 so that the response contains only the array
claude -p with an instruction to answer only in JSON, then parse stdout with a regex
explanation: Pairing a JSON schema with the JSON output format makes Claude constrain its output to that schema. The matching object lands in the structured_output field, where jq can pull it out. Asking for JSON in the prompt is not a constraint, and parsing stdout with a regex is fragile.

question: A CI job runs Claude headlessly to produce a migration plan. A separate job later must carry out that plan with the full context of the planning run. How should the two jobs be connected?
options: Pass the session_id from the first run's JSON output to claude --resume
Pipe the first run's stdout into the second run's stdin as its prompt
Run both steps in one claude -p call with a very large --max-turns value
Write the plan into CLAUDE.md so that the second run loads it automatically
explanation: For multi-step automation, capture the session ID from the JSON output and resume it later. The second run then has the planning session's full context. Piping stdout passes along only the final text, not the context behind it.

question: A CI pipeline needs Claude Code to give repeatable, predictable results on every run. Which flag does the course recommend for this?
options: --bare
--print
--resume
--output-format json
explanation: The course presents --bare as the mode for CI runs that need the same results every time. --print (-p) only makes a run one-shot and non-interactive. --resume continues an existing session.

question: A product team wants Claude Code's agent loop embedded inside its own Python application. The app should control which tools Claude may use, set a system prompt, and choose a permission mode in code. What fits?
options: A routine that the application triggers with an HTTP POST to the routine's API endpoint
Shelling out to claude -p from the app and parsing its plain-text stdout line by line
The Agent SDK query function with allowedTools, system prompt, and permission mode
The managed Code Review service with a custom trigger phrase
explanation: The Agent SDK embeds Claude Code in TypeScript or Python apps. It exposes a query function that takes the same options as the CLI and streams messages back. A routine runs on Anthropic's infrastructure, not inside your product.

question: A team automates a nightly job with Claude. It must read build artifacts that exist only on their internal CI runners and feed its results into the next script in their pipeline. Following the course's advice to start with routines and drop down only when needed, what should they use?
options: A routine, because the course makes routines the default for all repeat work
The managed Code Review service, configured to run on every push
Bypass permissions mode in a developer's interactive session
Headless claude -p in their pipeline, since the job needs their environment
explanation: Routines are the default, but they run from a fresh clone on Anthropic's infrastructure. When a job needs your own environment or logic around the run, you drop to headless mode. Treating "start with routines" as an absolute rule is the trap here.

question: A nightly headless Claude run in CI ends with text saying the migration "completed successfully." How should an automated check verify that run?
options: Check the run's JSON result and its process exit code
Parse the final prose for words like "successfully" or "failed"
Trust the summary, since auto mode's classifier reviewed every action
Ask a second headless run whether the first one succeeded
explanation: Headless runs should be verified by their JSON result and exit code, not by the wording of a summary. The auto-mode classifier only flags dangerous actions and never judges whether the work succeeded.

question: An org admin enables Anthropic's managed Code Review on several repositories. Which TWO statements describe how it behaves? (Select TWO.)
options: It approves PRs with no findings and blocks PRs that have severe ones
It posts findings as inline comments on specific lines, tagged by severity
It reviews only the changed lines, without looking at the rest of the codebase
It automatically pushes a fix commit for each finding that it posts
It never approves or blocks a PR, leaving the judgment call to a human
explanation: Code Review posts deduplicated inline findings tagged by severity, plus a summary table in the check run. It never approves or blocks, so a human makes the call. It analyzes the diff against the full codebase, and there is no managed autofix.

question: Managed Code Review flagged several issues on a developer's pull request, and the developer wants those findings applied to the code. What is the course's recommended flow?
options: Approve the Code Review check run so it commits its suggestions
Pull the branch and run /code-review --fix locally to apply the findings
Enable managed autofix in the Code Review section of admin settings
Comment @claude review again so the service pushes fixes to the PR
explanation: The managed service only posts findings and has no autofix. You apply findings locally: /code-review reviews a diff, and its --fix flag applies the findings to your working tree.

question: To control cost, a team wants managed Code Review to run only when a reviewer explicitly asks for it on a pull request. Which run setting fits?
options: Only on an @claude review comment
On a nightly cron schedule
Once automatically when each PR opens
Automatically on every push to the PR
explanation: The admin can set Code Review to run when a PR opens, on every push, or only when someone comments @claude review. The last option runs only on explicit request. A cron schedule is not one of its run settings.

question: A developer wants to set up the Claude Code GitHub Action on a repository, which includes installing the GitHub app and setting the API key secret. What is the starting point?
options: Ask an org admin to click Configure in the Code review settings
Run /install-github-app inside Claude Code with repo admin access
Run /schedule and choose a GitHub event as the trigger
Run /plugin install claude-code-action from any GitHub account
explanation: /install-github-app walks you through installing the GitHub app and setting the Anthropic API key secret, and it requires repo admin. The Configure button in admin settings sets up the separate managed Code Review service.

question: A team wants to comment "@claude implement the spec in the linked issue" on a pull request and have Claude push commits and post comments describing what it did. Which path fits?
options: A routine triggered whenever a pull request is opened
Running /code-review --fix on behalf of the PR author
Managed Code Review configured to run whenever someone comments @claude review
A claude-code-action@v1 workflow listening for the @claude trigger phrase
explanation: Managed Code Review only reviews and posts findings. When the job goes beyond review, such as implementing changes from a comment, you use the GitHub Action, which can push commits and post comments.

question: A scheduled GitHub workflow uses anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 to post a daily read-only report, and nobody watches it run. Which TWO claude_args adjustments does the course recommend? (Select TWO.)
options: Add --max-turns to put a hard cap on the agent loop
Set trigger_phrase to the cron expression for the schedule
Restrict allowed tools to the read-only ones the report needs
Use bypass permissions so that the job never stops to ask
Pass --resume so each day continues the previous day's session
explanation: claude_args is where you tune the run. A max-turns cap stops the loop from running forever, and allowed tools should be exactly what the job needs, which means read-only for a report. For a run with no one watching, the course recommends a permission mode that doesn't stop to ask, not bypass permissions, which belongs only in isolated containers or VMs.

question: A team runs Claude unattended in CI and wants test and lint results to be an actual gate, not something Claude merely claims to have checked. Which TWO hook setups does the course recommend? (Select TWO.)
options: A PostToolUse hook that lints and type-checks after every edit
A Stop hook that runs the tests and exits 2 on failure so Claude can't end the turn
A Notification hook that exits 2 when tests fail to halt the run
A CLAUDE.md rule reading IMPORTANT: always run the tests before finishing
A SessionStart hook that runs the full test suite once at startup
explanation: A Stop hook that refuses to end the turn on failure and a PostToolUse hook that lints and type-checks after each edit both run on every run, and exit 2 feeds failures back to Claude to fix. A CLAUDE.md rule is only a request. Notification ignores blocking, and a startup test run checks the code before any changes exist.

question: An app works locally but fails silently in production. The team wants Claude to find and fix production-only errors every day without anyone hunting through logs, while humans stay in control of what ships. Which design matches the automated-debugging workflow in the course?
options: Claude runs in bypass permissions on the production host and patches code in place as errors appear
Managed Code Review is enabled on main so it can detect and autofix runtime errors as they occur
A loop session polls CloudWatch every minute and pushes each fix straight to the main branch
A daily GitHub Action pulls CloudWatch logs; Claude dedupes errors, writes fixes, and opens a PR
explanation: In the course's workflow, a scheduled GitHub Action fetches recent CloudWatch logs, Claude deduplicates and analyzes the errors, and the proposed fixes arrive as a pull request for human review. Pushing directly to main or patching production removes that review step. Code Review has no autofix and doesn't read runtime logs.

question: A team has a polished .claude directory of skills, subagents, and hooks. Developers copy the files between machines, and the copies drift out of sync. What does the course recommend?
options: Move all of its content into the organization's managed policy CLAUDE.md
Convert each component into a routine so that it runs in the cloud
Package it as a plugin and publish it through a private team marketplace
Commit the directory to every repository and ask developers to pull it weekly
explanation: A plugin packages skills, subagents, hooks, and MCP configs as one versioned installable unit. A private marketplace gives the team central discovery, version tracking, and updates. Moving everything into CLAUDE.md turns enforceable hooks into mere guidance and bloats the always-loaded file.

question: A developer installs a community plugin for its skills. They already have their own PreToolUse hooks and a skill named review. Which TWO statements describe the result? (Select TWO.)
options: The plugin's hooks replace the developer's hooks for the same event
The plugin's skills are namespaced under the plugin name, so none clashes with review
Only the plugin's skills are enabled, and its hooks stay off until approved one by one
The developer's review skill is overwritten by any plugin skill with the same name
The plugin's PreToolUse hooks and the developer's own both fire on matching tool calls
explanation: Plugin components run alongside yours. Hooks stack, so both sets fire, and skills, agents, and commands are namespaced so they never clash. Installing a plugin for its skills also brings in its hooks, whether or not you read them.

question: After enabling a plugin, a developer notices that Claude Code's main thread now runs with a different system prompt, different tool restrictions, and a different model. What most likely caused this?
options: The plugin's settings.json agent key promoted one of its subagents to the main thread
The plugin shipped a CLAUDE.md that overrode the user and project CLAUDE.md files
The plugin's PreToolUse hook rewrote the model name in every tool call's input
Enabling any plugin replaces the user's settings.json with the plugin's own bundled copy
explanation: A plugin's settings.json is honored only narrowly: the agent key and the subagent status line key. The agent key promotes one of the plugin's subagents, with its system prompt, tool restrictions, and model, to the main thread. That is why the course says to look before you enable a plugin.

question: A plugin on the community marketplace passed Anthropic's automated review. A security-minded lead asks whether the team can install it without any further checks. What is the course's position?
options: No: community plugins can never be installed, only official ones
Yes, as long as the team uses only its skills and ignores its hooks
Yes, because automated review guarantees that the plugin's hooks are safe
No: reviewed isn't trusted, so inspect its hooks, agents, and MCP servers first
explanation: Automated review catches some problems, not all of them. A plugin runs code with your privileges, and its hooks fire whether or not you use them. You can't install a plugin for its skills and leave its hooks out.

question: A team is packaging its .claude setup as a plugin. Which TWO statements about the .claude-plugin/plugin.json manifest are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Name is its only required field, and the name namespaces the plugin's skills
Version is required, and installs fail whenever the version is omitted
It is optional, because components are discovered by directory convention without it
Every skill and hook must be listed in it, or Claude Code won't find them
It must live at .claude/settings.json inside the plugin's folder
explanation: The manifest is optional, because Claude Code discovers components by directory convention. When it is present, name is the only required field, and the name namespaces the plugin's skills. Versioning is recommended so updates can be tracked, but it isn't required.

question: Hours into a session, a developer has finished a long debugging detour and now only cares about the --version flag implementation. The context window is filling up. What is the best move?
options: Add the --version flag details to CLAUDE.md and keep going
Run /compact with no arguments and let Claude decide what to keep
Run /clear and re-explain the --version flag work from scratch
Run /compact Focus on the --version flag implementation
explanation: Compaction can drop something important. Text added after the command shapes what the summary keeps, which is your steering wheel for context. A bare /compact leaves that choice to the summary.

question: Claude spent several turns on a wrong approach and edited files badly. The discussion along the way was useful and the developer wants to keep it, but the file changes must be undone. Which rewind option fits?
options: Summarize from here
Restore code
Restore conversation
Restore code and conversation
explanation: Restore code rolls back only the files to the checkpoint and keeps the conversation. Restore code and conversation would also throw away the discussion the developer wants to keep.

question: A session began with a very long setup phase (environment wrangling and exploratory reads), followed by implementation work that the developer wants to keep in full detail. They need to free context space. Which rewind option should they choose at the checkpoint between the two phases?
options: Restore code and conversation
Summarize up to here
Restore conversation
Summarize from here
explanation: Summarize up to here compresses everything before the checkpoint, which is the setup phase, and keeps the implementation intact. Summarize from here does the opposite: it compresses what comes after the checkpoint, which suits a side conversation.

question: A developer sets /goal the billing service works correctly in production. Claude keeps working, but the goal never resolves sensibly. What is the core problem, and what is the fix?
options: Goals only work in plan mode, so switch to plan mode before setting the goal again
Goals accept only a single condition, so split it into two separate /goal commands
The evaluator reads only the transcript, so restate it as visible output like passing tests
The evaluator needs production access, so add a connector that queries the live service
explanation: A fast evaluator checks the goal by reading only the transcript, so the condition has to be checkable from output Claude produces, such as test runs or type-checker results. Giving the evaluator production access misreads how it works.

question: While working locally, a developer wants Claude to check a running CI pipeline at intervals between turns and act when its status changes. Which feature fits, and how is it stopped?
options: Loop, which is stopped by pressing escape
Rewind, which is stopped by double-tapping escape
Goal, which is stopped with /goal clear
A routine, which is stopped by deleting it on the web
explanation: Loop runs a prompt on a fixed or self-paced interval between turns, which suits polling external state like CI. Pressing escape stops it. A goal is a completion condition, not a polling mechanism.

question: A developer runs Claude sessions in separate worktrees. Each worktree is missing the git-ignored .env file the app needs, and the team does not want to commit that file. What solves this?
options: Remove .env from .gitignore so worktrees receive it
Use a SessionStart hook to print .env into context
List .env in a .worktreeinclude file at the repo root
Reference .env with an @-import in the project CLAUDE.md
explanation: A .worktreeinclude file at the repo root lists git-ignored files to copy into each worktree, such as env files or local config. Removing .env from .gitignore would risk committing secrets, which is what the team wants to avoid.

question: A developer wants several Claude Code instances building different features at the same time in one repository. Which TWO statements reflect the course's guidance? (Select TWO.)
options: Run every instance in one checkout and rely on rewind to undo collisions
A clean worktree is removed automatically when its session exits
Keep all but one instance in plan mode so only one writes at a time
Give each instance its own worktree so they can't clobber each other's files
Have all instances share one branch so that no merging is needed later
explanation: Several sessions in one file tree conflict with each other, like two steering wheels in one car. Worktrees give each session its own independent tree, and clean worktrees are removed automatically when the session exits. Serializing the work through plan mode gives up the parallelism the developer wants.

question: A developer keeps typing the same prompt to create a worktree for a named feature and start work in it. They want a reusable project command that takes the feature name as input. How should it be created?
options: As a markdown prompt file in .claude/commands using an $ARGUMENTS placeholder
As a line in CLAUDE.md that tells Claude to remember the prompt for later
As a routine triggered by an HTTP POST with the feature name in the body
As a PreToolUse hook that detects the phrase and expands it into the full prompt
explanation: Custom commands are markdown prompt files in .claude/commands, and the $ARGUMENTS placeholder fills in dynamic values like the feature name. A PreToolUse hook fires on tool calls, not on what the user types in a prompt.

question: A developer built a local MCP server that exposes a document-to-markdown tool and is started with uv run main.py. How do they make it available in Claude Code?
options: Run /goal with the startup command so Claude launches it as needed
Run claude mcp add documents "uv run main.py" and then restart Claude Code
Add the server's startup command as a new line in the project CLAUDE.md
Put main.py in a skill folder so Claude executes it as a script
explanation: You connect a server with claude mcp add followed by a name and a startup command, then restart Claude Code to get the new tools. A line in CLAUDE.md is only guidance and doesn't register any tools.

question: A developer opens an unfamiliar project in Claude Code. They want Claude to scan the codebase's architecture and coding style and record it as context that is included automatically in future requests. What should they run?
options: /init, which generates a CLAUDE.md file
/clear, which resets and re-reads the project
/goal, which records the project conventions
/compact, which summarizes the codebase
explanation: The init command scans the codebase for its architecture and coding style and writes a CLAUDE.md, which is included automatically in later requests. /compact summarizes the current conversation, not the codebase.

question: An unattended Claude run finished a large change overnight. Before merging, the team wants a review that catches what the original run may have talked itself past. What does the course recommend?
options: Ask the same session to carefully re-review all of its own changes before it closes
Read Claude's end-of-run summary and spot-check the files it lists
Re-run the task in auto mode so the classifier double-checks every action
Have a fresh session or subagent with no memory of the build review the changes
explanation: A reviewer with fresh context has no stake in the approach, so it catches what the author rationalized away. The original session carries those same rationalizations. The classifier judges only danger, never correctness.

question: Midway through a session, a developer realizes Claude took a wrong turn three prompts ago. They want to return to the state before that prompt rather than trying to prompt their way back out. How do they get there?
options: Press escape once while Claude is working, which reverts the most recent set of file edits
Run /goal clear so Claude abandons the current path and restarts from the original plan
Double-tap escape on an empty prompt and pick that prompt's checkpoint in the rewind menu
Run /compact so the wrong turn is summarized away, then continue from the summary
explanation: Every user prompt creates a checkpoint, and double-tapping escape on an empty prompt opens the rewind menu so you can go back to one. Compacting only summarizes the conversation. It doesn't undo the wrong path, and the bad file edits stay in place.

question: A developer presses shift-tab repeatedly, expecting eventually to land on don't ask or bypass permissions, but never sees either one. Which statement explains what they are seeing?
options: Shift-tab cycles the everyday modes (manual, accept edits, plan, auto); the status bar shows which is active
Shift-tab cycles all six modes, but only after auto mode has been approved for the current session
Shift-tab cycles all six modes, but don't ask and bypass are hidden from the status bar while active
Shift-tab only toggles between manual and plan, and every other mode needs its own slash command
explanation: Shift-tab cycles through manual, accept edits, plan, and auto, and the status bar always shows which mode is active. Don't ask and bypass permissions are not part of that everyday cycle. The status bar never hides the active mode.

topic: Creating a routine from the terminal
question: A developer working in Claude Code wants to set up a daily 9am dependency audit as a routine without leaving the terminal. What should they do?
options: Run /schedule and describe the job in plain language
Run /loop with a 24-hour interval so the audit repeats each morning
Run /goal with the audit as its completion condition so it recurs daily
Add a cron line to the project CLAUDE.md describing the audit schedule
explanation: Routines can be created on the web at claude.ai/code/routines or from inside Claude Code with /schedule and a plain-language description, such as "daily dependency audit at 9am". A loop runs between turns in your live session, so it isn't a cloud routine and stops when the session ends.

question: A team wants a routine that scans its Sentry tickets every morning and works out which issues in its repository are most urgent. When designing the routine, which set of things does it need to bundle?
options: A prompt, the repository, and a Sentry connector, plus a cron trigger
A skill folder, a Stop hook, and a developer's machine left running overnight
A prompt and a workflow file committed under the .github/workflows folder
A prompt, a server the team hosts, and an API key stored in CLAUDE.md
explanation: A routine ties together a prompt, the repository it works on, any connectors it needs (here, access to Sentry), and a trigger. There is no workflow file to maintain and no machine of yours to keep on, which is what sets routines apart from a GitHub Action.

question: A company's policy requires all model traffic to go through its Amazon Bedrock account. It wants to adopt anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 for @claude mentions on pull requests. Which action input addresses the policy?
options: github_token, replaced with a Bedrock access credential
trigger_phrase, set to a Bedrock-specific mention keyword
use_bedrock, which switches the action to that provider
prompt, with an instruction telling Claude to use Bedrock
explanation: The action has use_bedrock and use_vertex inputs for teams on those providers. The trigger phrase only controls which comment text the action listens for. Telling Claude to use Bedrock in the prompt doesn't change where requests are sent.

question: Inside a running session, a developer installs a plugin with /plugin install acme@release-tools. The install succeeds, but the plugin's skills don't seem to be available yet. What is the expected next step?
options: Add the plugin's skills to CLAUDE.md as @-imports
Run /reload-plugins to apply the change
Reinstall it through a private team marketplace
Run /init so that CLAUDE.md picks up the plugin
explanation: After /plugin install, Claude Code tells you to run /reload-plugins to apply the change. Plugin components are discovered from the plugin itself, so importing them into CLAUDE.md is unnecessary and would only add always-loaded text.

question: A team is turning its working .claude setup into a plugin and wants Claude Code to discover the components by convention. Which TWO placements match the course's plugin layout? (Select TWO.)
options: Hook definitions listed inside .claude-plugin/plugin.json
hooks/hooks.json and .mcp.json at the plugin root
Each subagent as its own markdown file under an agents folder
MCP server configs placed under each skill's own folder
All skills merged into a single skills.md at the plugin root
explanation: A plugin uses the same shape as .claude: one folder per skill, one markdown file per subagent under agents, and hooks/hooks.json plus .mcp.json at the plugin root. Claude Code finds components from that structure. The manifest only holds metadata such as name and version, so listing hooks there is the tempting mistake.

question: A platform team ships a plugin whose settings.json contains a broad set of preferences, including permission rules they expected every installer to inherit. After rollout, none of those permission rules take effect. What is the explanation?
options: Only the agent and subagent status line keys in a plugin's settings.json are honored
Plugin settings are always overridden whenever the project has its own CLAUDE.md file
Plugin settings take effect only when the plugin comes from the official curated marketplace
Plugin settings apply only after the user approves each key individually in the plugin panel
explanation: A plugin can ship a settings.json, but Claude Code reads only two keys from it: agent and the subagent status line. Other keys are ignored, so permission rules there do nothing. Where the plugin came from doesn't widen what is honored.

question: A team's SessionStart hook runs an expensive environment-priming script. They notice it also runs after every compaction, slowing long sessions down. They want it to run only when a session is freshly started. What should they configure?
options: Move the script into a PreToolUse hook on the Bash tool
Have the hook exit 2 whenever compaction triggers it
Move the script into a PostCompact hook instead
Limit the hook to the startup source of SessionStart
explanation: SessionStart fires in several situations, including right after compaction (the compact matcher). Using the startup source limits the hook to fresh starts. Exit 2 can't help, because SessionStart ignores blocking.

question: A team has a WorktreeCreate hook that runs a setup step. A minor lint warning in that step makes the script exit with code 1. The team expected exit 1 to be non-blocking, as it is for most hooks, but worktree creation fails. What explains this?
options: Exit 1 always blocks, and only exit 2 is treated as non-blocking
WorktreeCreate is an exception that aborts on any non-zero exit code
The .worktreeinclude file must list the hook script for it to pass
WorktreeCreate needs JSON with permissionDecision allow to proceed
explanation: For most events only exit 2 blocks, and other non-zero codes are just logged. The course's notes call out WorktreeCreate as an exception that aborts on any non-zero exit. Thinking exit 1 always blocks gets the general rule backwards.

question: A team already has a PreToolUse guardrail hook registered, but its logic runs on every tool call. They want it to inspect only git push commands. Which TWO configuration changes achieve this? (Select TWO.)
options: Add an if clause narrowing it to git push
Set the matcher to Stop so it fires at turn end
Re-register the hook on the PostToolUse event
Move the push rule into the project CLAUDE.md
Set the hook's matcher to the Bash tool
explanation: The matcher picks which tool to watch (Bash), and the optional if clause narrows the hook further to a specific command such as git push. PostToolUse is the tempting distractor, but it fires after the push has already happened, so it can't guard anything. CLAUDE.md is only guidance.

question: A team's claude-code-action workflow posts a rollup on a 9:00 UTC cron schedule. After a major incident, they want to run it immediately from the GitHub Actions tab instead of waiting until the next morning. What should the workflow include?
options: A second trigger_phrase matching the word incident
A workflow_dispatch trigger
A --max-turns value of zero passed in claude_args
A routine that mirrors the workflow on an HTTP trigger
explanation: Adding a workflow_dispatch trigger lets you start the scheduled workflow manually from the Actions tab. A trigger phrase applies only to @-mentions in PR and issue comments, not to manual runs.
